P1.evidence: P1a miss — no setter notes or application referenced at any point; the rep asks the prospect to supply everything from scratch. P1b partial — a two-part frame rather than the scripted four: 'I want to get a little bit deeper on what are you trying to get to, yeah? And what's been getting in the way.' That covers where you want to go and what's in the way, but not where you are now or what you need. P1c miss — no frame agreement sought, no 'does that work?'. P1d hit — clean and specific: 'if you could walk me through what's the biggest reason you reached out to us. What's the main thing you're trying to fix?'

P2.evidence: Two hits from nine. P2e hit — 'So currently, what do you do for training, only simple and sinister or something else?' produced a full picture including the squat rack and pull-ups. P2g hit and well run — 'Let's go into what nobody likes, which is nutrition. How does it look like for you right now?' followed by 'what's your typical day of eating look like?', surfacing the vegetarian protein problem, the snacking and the carb load. P2f partial — outcomes from Simple and Sinister were touched (progressed to the 32 kg bell, then boredom) but never framed as results. Everything else missing. P2a miss — no age, no height, no weight, despite fat loss being the prospect's first stated goal and 'I have a belly' being volunteered. P2b miss — his job surfaced only because he volunteered it mid-answer ('I'm an engineer, I code, develop things, I do a lot of financials, trading'); the rep never asked and later simply asserted it back. P2c miss — health conditions never asked. P2d miss and the most serious omission: injuries and movement limitations were never asked, and when the prospect volunteered a shoulder problem that stopped him training for two weeks ('I hurt like my shoulder wasn't feeling like it') the rep did not follow up at all, on a call selling a programme built around get-ups and overhead work. P2h miss — sleep never mentioned by anyone. P2i miss — energy never asked, despite 'have more energy' being one of his stated goals.

P3.evidence: Surface goals were captured but the surface-to-deep transition was asserted by the rep rather than excavated from the prospect. P3a/P3b partial — 'what's your main goal that you want to hit, actually?' is a single generic question standing in for the scripted aesthetics/function and mobility/strength/energy sequence; it did produce fat loss, muscle, strength, aches and energy in one answer. P3c partial — playing with the kids surfaced inside that same answer rather than being asked for. P3d miss — the bridge question 'outside of the physical, what's actually driving this right now?' was never asked. P3e miss — 'when you're moving better, what does that actually do for you?' never asked. P3f miss — 'who else does that impact?' never asked; the prospect volunteered his kids unprompted, which the script does not credit. P3g hit — the rep did drive through to family and identity, and did it well: 'you don't want to be that dad that's sitting on the couch with the remote', 'you're going to be leading by example', and later 'I think your family is a bigger why... You want to train with your son when he's going to be older. You want to play basketball with him and not just be on the sidelines.' P3h miss — no reflect-back; the rep never checked 'so this isn't really about the belly, it's about being the example — is that right?', which would have taken thirty seconds and was set up perfectly by the prospect's own 'I want to just exhibit good habits, I guess.'

P4.evidence: The strongest phase in the entire batch and a genuinely well-run piece of diagnosis. P4a hit — past attempts fully surfaced: Simple and Sinister, P90X, dumbbells, plyometrics, slow carb. P4b hit — outcomes for each drawn out, including 'I got in decent shape, I'd say, and then, you know, lost it.' P4c hit — asked directly and twice: 'what's the reason you cannot commit for longer? Is it that you're just getting bored with it, or what is it?' and 'How long have you been in this cycle and the spurts on and off?' P4d hit — 'in your own opinion, like what's the biggest gap between where you are right now and where you want to be?' P4e hit — the prospect named the gap himself, precisely and in his own words: 'I think it's the consistency... I have a bit of a perfection mindset', and later the deeper one, 'I've always done everything kind of on my own. I've never really hired a coach or anything, ever... I think that's probably one of my problems.' P4f hit and near-verbatim to the script: 'almost everybody knows what they should do. What to eat, that they should walk 10k steps a day, train, meditate and all of that. Everybody knows that. But who does that? This is the difference.' The prospect completed the thought himself — 'that's the accountability portion.'

P5.evidence: P5a hit — asked cleanly: 'what do you think, where is this going to go if you keep being on and off and not dialing that in?' But the phase was abandoned immediately afterwards. The prospect deflected into optimism and self-diagnosis ('that's not what I want to be, you know, so that's why I'm trying to... I think it's the mindset') and even talked himself UP, volunteering that he had been more consistent in recent months. The rep accepted that without pressing. P5b miss — 'is that something you're willing to settle for?' never asked. P5c miss — no 'why not?', so the prospect never articulated a cost of inaction in his own words. P5d miss — no line in the sand. Because the consequence was never made to bite, there was nothing to weigh against $6,000 forty minutes later.

P6.evidence: The best commitment check in the batch and the only properly delivered P6a. P6b hit — 'If we can figure out all the logistical details, like, are you actually fully committed to showing up and doing that work that needs to be done for you to be consistent and make that change?' answered 'I mean, I for sure am... in terms of commitment, I think I can commit.' P6a hit and correctly framed with the disqualifying consequence attached: 'do you feel that actually that can get you to your goals and that will make you consistent in the future? ... Because if you feel that it doesn't, it doesn't make sense for us to actually move forward.' The prospect answered substantively rather than reflexively. P6c hit — the rep waited for both answers before naming price. SEQUENCING: the three pillars were again presented (00:17:34 to 00:36:10) before the commitment check (00:38:26), which inverts the script's instruction, though the P6a belief question is necessarily about a presented programme, so the inversion is less damaging here than on the other calls.

P11.evidence: Payment and onboarding were never reachable — the prospect deferred to his wife and left for another meeting. Scored N/A so the rep is not penalised for an unreachable phase. However, the handover itself was materially worse than on the comparable Arturo call the previous day: no follow-up call was booked, no date proposed, no calendar invite sent. The rep closed with 'take your time. I'm going on vacation tomorrow. I'll be back in the second week of August, and we can pick it up there', leaving a warm prospect with a half-price offer on the table, no committed next contact and no owner for it. On the Arturo call the same rep booked live and verified the invite had arrived; that discipline was absent here.

objection_plays.detail: Started well and then collapsed into a discount. The isolation move ran and ran properly — 'Okay, but like with, you know, I can take a hint. Is it really finances or is there something else like you're not sure of?' — and the SHOULD/HOW reframe landed in substance: 'financials are only logistical things, and we can work around that.' The break-it-up offer ran: 'if we can make it more feasible for you in terms of structuring the payment, is that something that could potentially work for you?' Only one of the six financial-picture questions ran, and only obliquely — 'depending, like, what cache on hand you have right now that you could put down'. The prospect never gave a number. Monthly surplus, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, and investments were all skipped entirely. Instead of completing the picture, the rep introduced third-party financing (declined on principle) and then cut the price in half. The prospect had already said the money existed — 'I have that amount' — so the entire financial-picture sequence was arguably the wrong tool, but the play the rep reached for instead is not in the playbook at all.

Three of six moves. The rep pre-empted the objection before it was raised by role-playing the wife, which surfaced the obstacles the script asks about ('when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up?') though by performing them rather than asking for them. The key scripted question ran cleanly: 'do you feel that would be any reason that she wouldn't want you to actually, you know, finally live a healthier life? Because you're not doing it only for yourself, you're doing it for them' — answered 'Yeah, no, I don't think so. I think she's reasonable.' The rep also offered to join a joint call, which is not scripted but is sensible; the prospect declined. Three decisive moves did NOT run: 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal?', 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission to bet on yourself?', and 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house — is that responsibility hers or yours?'. The deposit-with-full-refund fallback was also not offered, despite the rep having already put a custom cash-down-plus-instalments structure on the table, which made it the natural next step.

Trigger raised explicitly — 'I got to think about that, to be honest' and later 'let me talk it over'. Two moves ran: the belief question was already banked at P6a, and 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?' ran twice in substance ('So what's coming up, apart from the finances? Like, does it check all the boxes for you?' and 'So what's coming up?'). The rest did not: no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?', and critically no 'that man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?', which was the obvious move given the rep had spent ten minutes building the be-an-example-to-your-son frame. No final 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?'

Doubt was present in two forms — wanting to see the programme before buying ('I need to see what the structure, see what the program is') and doubt about virtual versus in-person delivery. The scripted closing move ran almost verbatim and worked: 'How are you going to see it if you won't try it? ... you won't actually know until you try it, especially with fitness, because it's your body.' The prospect dropped that thread. None of the other OE moves ran — no certainty reframe, no pleasure/pain question, no bridge, no plane analogy. The virtual-versus-in-person doubt was answered with an unevidenced assertion ('Let's say it's even better because you cannot hire a coach for every single day. That would be probably astronomical') to a prospect who had just said he had no idea what coaching costs.
No timing objection. The prospect was ready to start and had a kettlebell workout planned for that same afternoon.

SCRIPT GAP — 'a cheaper alternative already worked for me'. This is the second documented instance of the gap the playbook already records from the Badrane Hriouch call, and here the substitute is not a rival coach but a book: Pavel's Simple and Sinister, which this prospect ran to the 32 kg bell for essentially zero cost. He describes it as 'good bang for buck'. The OC play assumes the blocker is capacity to pay; the actual competitor here is a functioning free programme, and its only failure mode was boredom, not ineffectiveness. Nobody built the case for why paid coaching beats the free thing that already worked — and the rep's eventual answer was to halve the price, which implicitly conceded the value argument.

SCRIPT GAP — the self-spend threshold. The prospect stated plainly that money was available and the barrier was psychological: 'I have that amount, but I don't think I've never spent that much ever on a coach ever. So I think that's the hurdle for me.' The rep correctly named it as a mindset blockade and the prospect agreed — and then the rep dropped the thread entirely and solved a cashflow problem instead. There is no play in the playbook for a buyer whose obstacle is crossing a first-time spending threshold on themselves, and this call shows exactly what happens without one: the price gets cut to meet a number that was never the objection.

SCRIPT GAP — virtual versus in-person delivery. 'It's all virtual, right? That's the difference, versus in person' was the prospect's first reaction to the price and it went unanswered by anything except assertion. This doubt sharpened moments earlier when the rep clarified that weekly check-ins are an in-app form rather than a call — 'no need to actually getting on a call with him' — which removed the live human contact the prospect was imagining. There is no scripted defence of the async delivery model.

notes: Two halves, and they point in opposite directions. The diagnosis was excellent: a complete P4 including the scripted 'everybody knows what to do, but who does that?' frame, and the only properly run P6a belief question in the batch. Then at the money stage the process stopped. The rep isolated the objection correctly, got the prospect to say out loud that the money existed and the barrier was a first-time self-spend threshold, and then abandoned that insight to solve for price — floating interest-bearing finance (declined), then inventing a $3,000 half-price tier with a different coach. Three concrete actions: (1) the $3,000 'light version' needs an immediate management ruling on whether it exists, because it was created live on this call; (2) when a prospect says 'I have that amount', stop running the financial-picture play and run the mindset play — which does not currently exist and should; (3) never end a warm call with a live offer and no booked next step, especially before a two-week absence. One safety note that sits outside the money story: the prospect volunteered a shoulder injury and it was never followed up on a call selling overhead kettlebell work.
